newsitem.title: USA: Key players in U.S. tobacco deal.
newsitem.headline: Key players in U.S. tobacco deal.

text.p: Key figures in the talks leading to Friday's landmark pact settling a torrent of U.S. anti-cigarette litigation were:

-- MICHAEL MOORE, the Mississippi attorney general, who filed the first state government suit in 1994 after a friend suggested he sue tobacco companies for Medicaid costs. A graduate of the University of Mississippi law school, he was a lead negotiator, and is a likely candidate for the Mississippi governship in 1999;

-- RICHARD SCRUGGS, a law school friend of Moore, was the lead outside lawyer representing attorneys general and a prime strategist in the talks. A former U.S. navy pilot, Scruggs made millions of dollars suing asbestos makers and is the brother-in-law of U.S. Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott;

-- RONALD MOTLEY a veteran liability lawyer who had scored well against health-device companies and others. A feared court performer, he has worn costumes to question witnesses and once rolled into a courtroom "the asbestos wheel of misfortune" in a case against asbestos firms;

-- STEVEN GOLDSTONE, a corporate lawyer named chief executive of RJR Nabisco Holdings in late 1995, opened the door to the talks last year by telling a British newspaper a broad solution was needed for the tobacco industry's legal woes;

-- BENNETT LEBOW, a financier now a pariah among tobacco executives, broke ranks by reaching separate settlements for the Liggett tobacco company owned by his Brooke Group Ltd. Documents that Liggett handed over to the attorneys general are believed to be especially harmful to the industry;

-- MERRELL WILLIAMS, an assistant at a Kentucky law firm who obtained copies of internal Brown & Williamson Tobacco Co. documents and delivered them to lawyers battling cigarette makers. A hero to anti-tobacco advocates, Williams is called a thief by tobacco-industry lawyers.
